seoDescription: Learn advanced composites techniques for creating a high-quality carbon fiber car bonnet or hood. This detailed tutorial covers the complete resin infusion process, from preparing the mold with a special epoxy-compatible polyester gel coat to achieve a perfect gloss finish, to the strategic layup of carbon fiber, a Soric core, and edge reinforcements. Master vacuum bagging best practices, including the infusion stack setup, drop tests, and precise resin flow control for a flawless, lightweight, and incredibly strong part.

chapters.title: Introduction and Gel Coat Application
chapters.description: The mold is prepared with a release agent and sprayed with a special epoxy-compatible polyester gel coat to achieve a perfect surface finish.

chapters.title: Preparing the Cured Gel Coat and Mold
chapters.description: After the gel coat cures overnight, the mold flange is cleaned for bagging tape and any high spots on the surface are sanded down.

chapters.title: Laying Up the Outer Skin Laminate
chapters.description: The complex laminate stack for the outer skin is laid into the mold, including carbon fiber, a Soric infusion core, and edge reinforcements.

chapters.title: Setting Up the Infusion Stack
chapters.description: All bagging consumables for the resin infusion process, including peel ply, infusion mesh, spiral wrap, and silicone connectors, are positioned on the layup.

chapters.title: Vacuum Bagging the Outer Skin
chapters.description: The vacuum bag is sealed over the layup, pleats are checked for slack, and the pump is connected via a catch pot to begin pulling a vacuum.

chapters.title: Performing the Infusion
chapters.description: After a successful vacuum drop test, epoxy resin with a blended hardener is mixed, degassed, and infused into the part under vacuum.

chapters.title: Completing Infusion and Curing
chapters.description: Resin flow is monitored as it progresses through the Soric core, and once the part is fully saturated, the lines are clamped for curing.

chapters.title: Demolding the Outer Skin
chapters.description: Once cured, the bagging materials are stripped off and the flawless, high-gloss carbon fiber outer bonnet skin is removed from the mold.

chapters.title: Preparing and Laying Up the Inner Skin
chapters.description: Work begins on the inner bonnet skin, laying up a lighter two-layer laminate of 200g and 660g carbon fiber directly onto the prepared mold.

chapters.title: Bagging and Infusing the Inner Skin
chapters.description: The inner skin layup is prepared with a standard infusion stack, vacuum bagged, leak tested, and then infused with epoxy resin.

chapters.title: Demolding the Inner Skin and Conclusion
chapters.description: After the resin has infused and cured, the inner skin is demolded, revealing a strong and lightweight part, and the next steps are outlined.

summary:
## Key Concepts for Carbon Fiber Bonnet Resin Infusion

This document outlines the key stages and materials used to create the outer and inner skins of a carbon fiber bonnet via resin infusion.

### Mold Preparation & Surface Finish

- **Release Agent**: The mold surface is first prepared with several coats of a chemical release agent to ensure the finished part can be easily removed.
- **Epoxy-Compatible Gel Coat**: A special clear polyester gel coat (**GC50**) is sprayed onto the mold surface. This provides a durable, high-gloss, pinhole-free finish for the final part.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Do not use a standard polyester gel coat with epoxy resin. It will fail to bond and cause immediate delamination. The **GC50** is specifically formulated for compatibility.

- **Curing & Prep**: The gel coat is cured overnight. It cures to a hard, tack-free finish. Before lamination, any overspray on the flanges is cleaned, and any drips or high spots on the gel coat surface are sanded flat.

### Outer Skin Laminate & Layup

The outer skin is a sandwich construction designed for stiffness and a perfect cosmetic finish.

- **Laminate Schedule**:
  1.  **First Layer**: One ply of **200g 2x2 Twill Carbon Fiber** for the cosmetic surface.
  2.  **Core**: One layer of **2mm Soric Infusion Core**. This material adds thickness and stiffness while acting as an internal flow medium for the resin.
  3.  **Edge Reinforcement**: Six layers of **200g Carbon Fiber Tape** are applied around the perimeter, butting up against the Soric core to create a solid carbon edge with matching thickness.
  4.  **Final Layer**: One ply of **200g Carbon Fiber** over the entire surface.

> [!TIP]
A light spritz of **acetone** on the carbon can temporarily activate the gel coat surface, helping to hold the fabric in place during layup.

- **Positioning**: **Infusion-grade spray tack** is used to accurately position the Soric core and carbon tape reinforcements.

### Inner Skin Laminate & Layup

The inner skin is designed for strength and low weight.

- **Laminate Schedule**:
  1.  **First Layer**: One ply of **200g Carbon Fiber** for a clean surface finish.
  2.  **Second Layer**: One ply of **660g Carbon Fiber**. This provides significant thickness and strength in a single, cost-effective layer.

> [!NOTE]
> The inner skin molding does not use a gel coat. Spray tack is used to position the fabric, which may leave minor cosmetic imperfections not visible on the final assembly.

### Resin Infusion Process

1.  **Infusion Stack**: After the reinforcement is laid, the infusion stack is applied in order:
    *   **Peel Ply**: A textured fabric that leaves a peelable, bonded surface and absorbs excess resin.
    *   **Infusion Mesh**: A plastic mesh that creates a high-flow channel for resin over the top of the part.
    *   **Spiral Wrap**: Used along the feed and vacuum lines to ensure even distribution.
    *   **Silicone Connectors**: For attaching resin and vacuum lines.
    *   **Vacuum Bag**: Sealed around the mold perimeter with bagging tape.

2.  **Vacuum Drop Test**: Before introducing resin, the sealed bag is put under full vacuum, and the pump is isolated. The vacuum gauge is monitored for at least 30 minutes. **No drop in vacuum is acceptable.** This is a critical step to ensure a leak-free system.

3.  **Resin & Hardener**: The **IN2 Epoxy Infusion Resin** is used. A **50/50 blend of Fast and Slow hardener** creates a medium pot-life, ideal for a part of this size. The resin must be mixed thoroughly but gently to avoid introducing air.

4.  **Infusion**: With the pump running, the resin feed line is unclamped. The vacuum draws resin into the part, flowing along the spiral wrap and through the Soric core and infusion mesh.

5.  **Completion**: Once the part is fully saturated and resin begins to enter the vacuum line, the **resin feed line is clamped first**, followed by the **vacuum line**. This isolates the part under vacuum to cure.

### Demolding

- After a full cure (approx. 24 hours), the bagging materials are stripped away.
- The peel ply is removed from the back of the part.
- The finished carbon fiber part is then carefully released and removed from the mold.
transcription:
## Introduction and Gel Coat Application

Hello and welcome to the next installment in this video tutorial series. In this installment, we're going to be actually making the carbon fiber bonnet itself. We're going to be showing you the latest techniques for making a medium-sized carbon fiber panel like this. And obviously, we're using the mold that we made earlier in the series.

The first thing that we've done is prepare the surface of this mold using several applications of easy chemical release agent, which we've done as per the instructions for that product. And now the next thing that we're going to do is an optional step, but we're actually going to spray the surface of this mold using a very special epoxy compatible polyester gel coat.

Now, it's very important at this point that we make it very clear that the GC50 epoxy compatible polyester gel that we're spraying here is not the same as a normal polyester gel coat. Please don't try and use a normal polyester gel with epoxy because it just simply will not bond and will immediately delaminate.

However, one thing it does have in common with a normal polyester gel is the fact that we catalyze it using a regular MEKP catalyst. We've mixed the gel up in one of the paper cups that's designed for the cup gun. So, it's a case of just putting that cup into the holder and then pressing the lid firmly on. And then we load this into the gun by pulling the spring to hold the cup in place.

Our gel coat spraying cup gun is equipped with a 6 mil nozzle, which when you're spraying a material as viscous as a gel coat, is the ideal choice. And we're just going to try and get a smooth, even coat over the surface, starting and finishing off the edge of the part to avoid getting any drips on the mold.

## Preparing the Cured Gel Coat and Mold

We've now allowed this gel coat to cure fully overnight. Now, unlike a conventional polyester gel coat, when this cures, it cures with a hard finish and no tack at all. And that leaves the perfect bonding finish for the epoxy resin. So, the first thing that we're going to do is just wipe around the perimeter of the mold, clearing any overspray off this flange. And that's so that we've got a nice clean surface to stick the bagging tape onto. 

We're going to apply the bagging tape all the way around the perimeter of the mold at this point for convenience really before we put down the bagging consumables and the reinforcement itself. The only other thing that we're going to do before we start is we're just going to look for any high spots like this on the mold surface which have been caused by a drip off the gel coat gun and we're just going to flat those off and that will stop any of these from printing through onto the surface of the reinforcement.

## Laying Up the Outer Skin Laminate

We're going for a laminate of 200 g carbon, 2 mil Soric, and then 200 g carbon.

Visually, of course, the first layer is the most important. So, we're just being careful to gently drape this two-twill into the mold. Often what you want to do is get the carbon to just stick slightly in position. And so what we do is just spritz a very small amount of acetone onto the carbon. And what that does, it just slightly activates the gel coat surface and means that you can stick the carbon down onto it.

And once we've done that, we just use a pair of shears to cut off the excess material. We've only got to be just inside of the tape line.

And now this is the Soric, which is an infusion core material. And we've cut this just with a pair of scissors about 25 mil short of the edge of the bonnet all the way around. And that's just because we don't want the core material exposed at the edge of the panel. In this closeup, you can really see and get a good idea of how the Soric core material feels and behaves. It's very easy to cut and lay into the mold. And then we've got this fine honeycomb structure around which the resin can flow as an internal core media.

Next, we're using some special infusion grade spray tack and just spraying that lightly over the surface of the reinforcement and then using that to help us position the Soric squarely and evenly in the middle of the mold, which is quite important for us because we want to maintain an even gap all the way around the edge where the core material ends. because into that we're going to be layering some 200 g carbon tape.

We're using a 50 mil tape here. Again, the infusion spray tack is particularly helpful to allow us to fix that in place and position it very accurately up against the edge of the soric. We certainly don't want a gap at this point. We're going to build up six layers of the carbon tape so that we've got a match for the thickness of the Soric. So you can see we've got this tape nice and neatly butted up against the Soric. So we're just going to add our next layer, final layer of 200 g carbon cloth all the way over the surface.

And then we're just going to trim this just like we did before.

## Setting Up the Infusion Stack

So over the top of this second layer of reinforcement, we're just positioning a layer of peel ply. And we're just going to hold this in place with a few pieces of the release breaker tape.

The next thing that we want to be thinking about is the infusion mesh and the spiral. So, we're going to position infusion mesh along the front here because we're going to be running the resin the shortest distance, which is from the back of the bonnet to the front of the bonnet.

And then we'll also be positioning another strip of the infusion mesh just at this front edge. And that's going to help to spread the vacuum. We're positioning this infusion spiral all the way around this back edge and just holding it in place with some of the release breaker. So, the final thing to do before we bag this up is to position the resin infusion silicon connectors. We've got one here at the back of the bonnet, which is the resin feed line. So, that sits on top of the spiral. And then we've got one opposite on the front end of the bonnet, which sits on this mesh, and this is the vacuum line. So, we're just going to tape that in place to stop it moving down and just pierce through.

We've added some gum tape pleat around the outside of the of the mold. And so, we're just sealing this bag down to the tape.

## Vacuum Bagging the Outer Skin

Now, we've got an alternative video dedicated to the vacuum bagging process, so we're not going to cover it in much detail here. But if I just go over what we've got, we've got the vacuum bag completely sealed to the tool all the way around. We've got our pleats in place, ensuring that we've got plenty of bag, plenty of slack on the bag. At the top of the bonnet here, we've got the vacuum line connected to the catch pot and the catch pot connected to the composite's vacuum pump. And then where we've got the resin feed line at the back of the bonnet, this is just clamped off. So, what we're going to do is switch the vacuum pump on and pull a vacuum on this.

## Performing the Infusion

Finally, before we can infuse, we're just going to clamp off this bag and do a vacuum drop test, which is absolutely essential before we can do the infusion.

We've come back to this part now a couple of hours later and we've performed the vacuum drop test and that's shown us that there's been absolutely no pressure drop in this bag whatsoever. And so that's the point where we can continue when you're calculating the amount of resin that an infusion project's going to use. Of course, you do need to make sure that you allow for the the Soric and also the vacuum bagging consumables. We've actually got a handy calculator on the Easy Composites website that will help you to do this. Now, you'll see us do this again later, but what we're doing here is just mixing a 50/50 blend of the fast and the slow hardener, which are available for the IN2 infusion resin. And the reason we do that is this gives us a medium speed hardener, which is perfect for an infusion of this size. It's very important to thoroughly mix the resin with its hardener, trying to do so without aerating the resin while we do it, but any unmixed resin will fail to cure in the part.

So, we've allowed the resin just to degass for a few minutes just to get any large air bubbles out. So, what we're going to do is release the clamp from the vacuum line from when we did the drop test. Going to turn on the vacuum pump, open the vacuum pump supply, and then we're just going to draw the first amount of resin up to this clamp just to remove any air that's in at this point.

## Completing Infusion and Curing

We're just using one of the spare clamps to hold the line on the side of the resin container. And then we just gently unclamp the resin line into the part. You can see how quickly the resin follows the line of the feed spiral, giving it a very even advance across the part.

So you can see how effective the Soric is as an internal flow media because this line here where the resin advancing through the part is not being hindered by the fact that the infusion mesh is actually stopped at this point and this is still progressing through the laminate nicely.

As you can see, the resin has now reached the silicon connector on the other side of the part, and the resin is actually starting to be drawn down the vacuum line. So, what we're going to do is just let this carry on being drawn just for a couple of minutes, and that's actually extracting some of this aerated resin. And then we're going to clamp off the resin line.

With both of these lines clamped off, now we're okay to turn off the vacuum pump and we're going to leave this part to fully cure. Now, with the hardener speed that we've chosen and the ambient temperature, that's going to take about 24 hours.

## Demolding the Outer Skin

With this part now completely cured off, you can hear the resin is absolutely solid. It's now time to remove all of the bagging consumables from the mold. So, we're going to start with the uh the bag itself. Just removing the peel ply from the back of this laminate has actually started to pre-release it from the mold already. So, we know we're not going to have any trouble. And that really is the sign of a good chemical release agent. So, we're just going to get in and and tease it up. And it's it's out of the mold already.

With this part out of the mold, you can really see all of this hard work's paid off. We've got a fantastic mirror gloss over the surface of the bonnet uh from that uh clear gel coat that we've used. There's no pin holes whatsoever. There's no bubbles. There's no air inclusions. And uh so you've got to be pretty pleased with that at this stage.

## Preparing and Laying Up the Inner Skin

Moving on now to the inner skin molding. We're actually going to be using uh just two layers of reinforcement on this, which is going to be a 200 g and a 600 g because we want this to be as light as possible. Although, we're going to have additional reinforcement in the critical areas, which is where the hinges are and also where the catch mechanism is at the top. This mold has been prepared with several applications of easy chemical release agent just like we've done in previous sections. And so, we'll just be laying on the reinforcement directly onto that.

So the 200 g cloth is the first one down onto the mold because obviously this has the the flatter finish. We're going to use some spray tac just on the surface of the of the mold. And this will help us to position the uh the carbon. Now it will leave slight imperfections on the surface of the part but that doesn't matter for the underside molding that we're working on here.

The next step is to put our second layer of reinforcement down. So in this case we're using the 660 g cloth. Now the reason for doing that is that this will actually give us about 6 nearly 7 mil thickness of reinforcement. Uh, but we can do it in a single layer, which is not only quicker to put down, but it's also considerably cheaper than three or more layers of a 200 gram cloth. Another light application of the spray tack will just help us to position this heavier 660 g cloth.

With both layers of reinforcement down, now we're just going to trim away the excess reinforcement.

## Bagging and Infusing the Inner Skin

With all of our reinforcement in place, we'll just now go on with a standard infusion vacuum bagging stack, which will be peel ply, then the mesh, and then the bag itself. We're just going to cut the mesh approximately to the right size. And then we're just going to hold it loosely in place. We're going to take some of the vacuum bagging tape and just tape up all the way around the edge of the flange. As before, we're just going to add a few pleats made out of the bagging tape and position these around the edges.

The next thing we've done is position the infusion spiral around this uh this edge. And we've also gone down the sides as well in exactly the same pattern that we did for the top skin. So, we're just going to position the infusion silicon connector on top of the spiral here. And then we've got the other infusion connector ready to go at the front. And so on now with the bagging film itself, which we're going to tape down onto these pleats.

So, we're going to switch on the vacuum pump, start to pull the bag down, and position the bag as it goes down. Now, clearly, we've sped up time quite a bit in this shot, but this really is a very important part of the uh resin infusion process. And for that reason, if you want to learn more about how to get the bag down properly, then please check out our resin infusion video and our video dedicated to vacuum bagging. 

We've completed the drop test. now on this bag. So, we're 100% confident that there is no leak whatsoever. So, it's now time to do the infusion itself. So, as before, we're going to be using an epoxy infusion resin. And for this infusion, cuz it's going to take place relatively quickly, we're actually going to be using a combination of the fast and the slow hardener together. With the resin thoroughly mixed now and settled, it's time to start the infusion.

Start the vacuum.

## Demolding the Inner Skin and Conclusion

As you can see, the resin has now reached the other side of the infusion project. So, it's time to clamp off the feed line. And we can now clamp off the resin line. So, we can now turn off the vacuum pump and leave this to cure overnight or as long as it takes depending on the hardness speed that we've used.

We've now left this part to fully cure and so it's time to strip off all of the vacuum bagging consumables just like normal. With everything stripped off now, we'll just remove the uh the part from the mold. And that is our inner molding. Now that we've got the uh mold out of the way, we can have a nice look at this part itself. It really is incredibly strong and light. And uh all of the detail that we've got on the on the underside molding, of course, has been faithfully reproduced in this uh in this inner skin. So, this is going to make a fantastic inside for our bonnet.

We've now made both the outside skin and the inside skin for our carbon fiber bonnet. And so that concludes this part of the video tutorial. In the final part, we'll be looking at trimming both of these components, fixing the uh the fittings inside, and then bonding them together, and finishing it to complete the part.
